items.name: Readability
items.evidence: Names are mostly clear (apex_frame, y_stance_pre, takeoff_candidates) and there are some comments. But analyze_jump has no docstring, and it uses cryptic names in the business logic: h, w, f, f16, k5, bot_y, p99_y. The 115-line function body has no internal sections.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: analyze_jump is about 115 lines (cap: one function over 100 lines). It does video loading, background subtraction, per-frame stats and takeoff/landing detection all at once, against the convention of separate signal and detection functions. The pre/post window and candidate logic is copy-pasted.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: It checks cap.isOpened() and raises ValueError for too few frames or no runner, and it never swallows errors. But it is full of magic constants that are not named: >30, len(ys)>=300, order[:30], apex±12/±2, tol 8.0, 100/420/10/950 ROI, fallbacks apex_frame-5 and +4.

items.name: Robust to bad inputs and missing detections
items.name_zh: 异常输入与检测失败的处理
items.evidence: It validates opening and raises ValueError on 'No runner detected' (the traceback means a non-zero exit). But the thresholds are absolute pixel values, only scaled by h/540. If no candidates are found it silently writes made-up frames: 'takeoff_frame = apex_frame - 5', 'land_frame = apex_frame + 4'.

items.name: Output contract honoured
items.evidence: It reads the first positional argument as the video path, writes /app/output.toml by default with exactly two int() fields under the right names, and uses 0-based frame indices consistently. Hidden tests passed.
